explanations.answer: Men to spy out the land
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, “Send out for yourself men to spy out the land of Canaan…” (Numbers 13:2). These men are going to look around and bring back what they see. Scouts, not soldiers.

explanations.answer: An army to take the land
explanations.explanation: An army sounds big and exciting, I get it. But the LORD says to send men to spy out the land (Numbers 13:2). Spying means looking around, and nobody is told to swing anything. Moses, Israel's leader, gets scouts, not soldiers.

Nice thought, friend, but no peace talks are on the schedule. The LORD tells Moses to send men to spy out the land (Numbers 13:2). A messenger shows up with a speech, but a spy comes back with information. This trip is about looking.

Right on the money, baker. The LORD says, “From each of their fathers’ tribes send one man who is a leader among them.” (Numbers 13:2). So every tribe gets a seat on this trip. Nobody gets left standing at the curb.

Not quite, friend. The text says the LORD tells Moses, “From each of their fathers’ tribes send one man who is a leader among them.” (Numbers 13:2). One man from each tribe, and every one of them a leader. That's how the roster ends up with so many different names.

explanations.answer: How strong they are and how many
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Moses tells the spies to see “whether its people are strong or weak, few or many.” (Numbers 13:18). He wants to know the size of the crowd and the strength of the crowd. Remember that question, because the answers come back later.

explanations.answer: What language they speak at home
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, friend, but Moses never asks about that. He tells the spies to see “whether its people are strong or weak, few or many.” (Numbers 13:18). It's about strength and numbers. Dinner table conversation isn't on the list.

explanations.answer: Which gods they bow down to
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to wonder, but it isn't what Moses asks here. His words are to see “whether its people are strong or weak, few or many.” (Numbers 13:18). The questions are about strength and numbers. I'd stick to what Moses actually says.

Yes, baker! Moses asks, “Are the cities where they dwell open camps or fortifications?” (Numbers 13:19). He wants to know if those cities are wide open or walled in. Good question, since you'd want to know that before knocking on any door.

Close, but Moses really does ask this. He says, “Are the cities where they dwell open camps or fortifications?” (Numbers 13:19). So the spies have to look at the cities too, not only the people. Back to the cookie sheet, friend, it's still in the text.

Fruit it is, baker! Moses says, “Be courageous and bring back some of the fruit of the land.” (Numbers 13:20). A taste of the land, so everyone back home can see it for themselves. Notice he says to be courageous, too.

Stones, friend? I get why that came to mind, but that's not what Moses says. He tells them to “bring back some of the fruit of the land.” (Numbers 13:20). I bake with a lot of things, and rocks have never made the recipe.

A reasonable guess, but Moses doesn't ask for water. He says, “Be courageous and bring back some of the fruit of the land.” (Numbers 13:20). They're bringing back something you can hold up and show people. That's the fruit.
That's right, baker. The text calls Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai “the descendants of Anak” (Numbers 13:22). They live in Hebron. Keep the name Anak in your pocket, because it comes up again.
Lot was Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5), so I see why a famous name came to mind. But here the text names someone else. Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai are “the descendants of Anak” (Numbers 13:22).

Esau was Jacob's twin brother (Genesis 25:24-26), and a lot of people know that name. Still, that's not who the text says. It calls Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai “the descendants of Anak” (Numbers 13:22).

explanations.answer: On a pole between two men
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The text says they cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes, “which they carried on a pole between two men.” (Numbers 13:23). One pole, two men, one cluster. That cluster was not a snack-size situation.

explanations.answer: In a basket on one man's back
explanations.explanation: One man with a basket sounds simple, but it's not what happened. The text says the cluster was “carried on a pole between two men.” (Numbers 13:23). If one man could have carried it, I think the second man would have been delighted to hear that.

explanations.answer: Tied to the side of a donkey
explanations.explanation: A donkey would have been a nice helper, friend, but no donkey shows up in this verse. The text says they “carried on a pole between two men.” (Numbers 13:23). The men did the carrying themselves.

Almost, friend, but grapes weren't the only fruit. The text says, “They also took some pomegranates and figs.” (Numbers 13:23). So the spies came home with a whole fruit sampler. The grapes just got the most attention.
That's right, baker! Besides the grapes, “They also took some pomegranates and figs.” (Numbers 13:23). The cluster gets the big headline, but it had company. Quite a haul from one valley.

You got it, baker! The spies tell Moses, “…it is flowing with milk and honey.” (Numbers 13:27). They start with good news and they have the fruit right there to show it. Hold onto this part, because the report is about to turn.

That's not what the spies say, friend. They tell Moses, “…it is flowing with milk and honey.” (Numbers 13:27). They even say, “Here is some of its fruit!” Hard to call a land thorny with all that fruit in your hands.
Not this time, baker. The spies say, “…it is flowing with milk and honey.” (Numbers 13:27). They hold up the fruit as proof. Nobody is saying small or rocky at this point in the report.

Right, baker. The spies say, “…the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified.” (Numbers 13:28). Remember Moses asked if the people were strong or weak (Numbers 13:18). Now they're giving him their answer.

I see where you're going, friend, but that's not the report. The spies say, “…the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified.” (Numbers 13:28). Moses did ask whether the people were strong or weak (Numbers 13:18). They answered strong.

Peaceful would have been a nice thing to hear, but the spies don't say it. They say, “…the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified.” (Numbers 13:28). Nothing in the report mentions peace. That word never comes up.

That's him, baker! The text says, “Then Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said…” (Numbers 13:30). Caleb is the spy from the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6). When the mood in the room gets noisy, he stands up and speaks.

Shammua is a real spy on the list, from the tribe of Reuben (Numbers 13:4). But the text doesn't say he's the one who quieted the people. It says, “Then Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said…” (Numbers 13:30).

Sethur is on the roster too, from the tribe of Asher (Numbers 13:13). But he isn't the one who steps up here. The text says, “Then Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said…” (Numbers 13:30). Good memory for a name, though.
Yes, baker! Caleb says, “We must go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly conquer it!” (Numbers 13:30). He doesn't say maybe, and he doesn't say we'll see. He says certainly.

Buying the land would be a very different trip, friend. Caleb says, “We must go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly conquer it!” (Numbers 13:30). His word is conquer. No receipts needed.

Sharing sounds friendly, baker, but that's not Caleb's word. He says, “We must go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly conquer it!” (Numbers 13:30). He's talking about going up and taking it. I think he's sure of himself.

That's right, baker. The text says, “So they gave the Israelites a bad report about the land that they had spied out…” (Numbers 13:32). These are the men who answered Caleb with, “We cannot go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are!” (Numbers 13:31). Caleb said go, and they said no.

Not this time, friend. The text says, “So they gave the Israelites a bad report about the land that they had spied out…” (Numbers 13:32). Those men had just told Caleb, “We cannot go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are!” (Numbers 13:31). The report that followed was a bad one.

Careful there, baker, because that's not in their report. They say, “The land we explored devours its inhabitants, and all the people we saw there are great in stature.” (Numbers 13:32). Nothing about dry soil. Earlier they even said the land is “flowing with milk and honey” (Numbers 13:27).

Right, baker! Their bad report says, “The land we explored devours its inhabitants, and all the people we saw there are great in stature.” (Numbers 13:32). They never call it too dry to grow anything. They had already said it's “flowing with milk and honey” (Numbers 13:27), and they brought the fruit to prove it.

That's the one, baker. They say, “We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight…” (Numbers 13:33). That's how small they felt next to the people they saw. I think a grasshopper standing next to a mountain would understand that feeling.

Little children is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the picture they use. They say, “We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight…” (Numbers 13:33). It's a much smaller picture than children. Tiny bugs, jumping around.

Sheep is a reasonable guess, baker, but the text goes smaller. They say, “We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight…” (Numbers 13:33). A grasshopper is a lot smaller than a sheep. That tells you how small they felt.
